lead: A list comprehension builds a new list out of a loop, an optional filter and an expression, all on one line. Instead of creating an empty list, writing a for loop and calling append again and again, you write the transformation once and say which items it applies to. The result is a fresh list, so the original data is untouched. Python programmers use it constantly for small conversions: turning rupee amounts into paise, pulling names out of database rows, squaring a set of marks, keeping only the entries that pass a test.
prereq: You need: 3.3 Lists for creating, appending to and aliasing lists, and the for loop with range() from Unit 2.

sections.h3: The shape of a list comprehension

blocks.text: A list comprehension is a loop and an append squeezed into one expression. The loop walks an iterable, computes one value for each item, and appends that value to a new list.

blocks.where: expr is the value stored, computed from item; item is the loop variable, a new name bound to each element in turn; iterable is anything a for loop can walk, such as range(1, 7), a string, or d.items() for a dictionary d. The brackets make one expression whose value is a new list.

items: Evaluate the iterable once. range(1, 7) gives 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
Bind item to the first value and compute expr.
Append that result to the new list.
Repeat for the remaining values, in order.
Return the new list. The original iterable keeps its contents and its identity.

blocks.text: The loop version and the comprehension version give the same list. Compare them side by side:

blocks.code:
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
doubled = []
for x in numbers:
    doubled.append(x * 2)
print(doubled)
print([x * 2 for x in numbers])

blocks.text: Both printed lines are identical. The comprehension is shorter, but it does the same three things: loop, compute, append.

sections.h3: Filters, if-else inside the expression, and nesting

blocks.text: Add an if clause and the loop keeps only the items that pass the test. The item is computed only when the condition is true.
[expr for item in iterable if cond]
blocks.where: cond is any boolean expression written in terms of item. Items where cond is False are skipped completely; they never reach expr, so the new list is shorter than the old one.

blocks.text: The writing order inside the brackets is fixed: expression first, then the for clause, then the if clause. The expression itself may hold a conditional of the form a if c else b. That conditional is not a filter; it decides which value is stored for an item that is already being processed.

head: Form
Example
Result
rows: [expr for x in it if cond]
[a if c else b for x in it]
[x if x > 0 else 0 for x in [-1, 2]]
[i + j for i in range(1, 3) for j in range(1, 3)]

blocks.text: Two for clauses act exactly like nested loops. The leftmost for is the outer loop and the next one is the inner loop. For i = 1 the inner loop gives j = 1 then j = 2, producing 2 and 3. For i = 2 it produces 3 and 4. The list fills as [2, 3, 3, 4]. Swapping the two for clauses changes the order of the results.
The if-else form needs its else. [x if x > 0 for x in data] is a SyntaxError, because the parser sees a conditional expression and finds no else to complete it.

sections.h3: Reading the result, and keeping it readable

blocks.text: A comprehension always creates a new list object. If another name points at the old list (see 3.3 Lists), the old list is not modified.

blocks.code:
marks = [45, 72, 30]
new = [m + 5 for m in marks]
print(marks)
print(new)
print(marks is new)

blocks.text: Any iterable works as the source: a range, a string (each item is one character), or a dictionary's items, where each item is a key-value pair that you unpack into two names.

blocks.code:
word = "delhi"
print([c.upper() for c in word])
price = {"pen": 10, "book": 40}
print([name for name, cost in price.items() if cost > 20])

blocks.text: Keep to one or two clauses. A line with three for clauses and two filters is correct but hard to debug, because you cannot print an intermediate value inside it. Write the plain loop instead and let the reader follow it.

Set and dictionary comprehensions reuse the same pattern with braces and a key-value pair; they are covered in 3.7 Sets and 3.6 Dictionaries. Generator expressions, which produce values one at a time instead of building a list, belong to Unit 4.

figure.caption: The numbers 1 to 6 pass through the loop and the even filter; only 2, 4 and 6 reach the expression and become 4, 16 and 36.

spec.title: x * x for even x in 1 to 6
spec.aria: A left-to-right flow from the numbers 1 to 6 through a for clause and an even-number filter to the squared values 4, 16 and 36.

examples.question: Write the output of each list comprehension, with one line of reasoning each. (a) [x*x for x in range(1, 7) if x % 2 == 0]  (b) [x if x > 0 else 0 for x in [-2, 3, -1, 5]]  (c) [i + j for i in range(1, 3) for j in range(1, 3)]
steps: (a) range(1, 7) gives 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. The filter x % 2 == 0 is true only for 2, 4 and 6.
(a) Those three values reach x*x: 2*2 = 4, 4*4 = 16, 6*6 = 36. Output [4, 16, 36].
(b) Here the if-else sits in the expression, so no item is dropped. The list has four items: -2, 3, -1, 5.
(b) -2 is not greater than 0, so store 0. 3 > 0, store 3. -1 is not greater than 0, store 0. 5 > 0, store 5. Output [0, 3, 0, 5].
(c) The first for is the outer loop, i = 1 then i = 2. The second for is the inner loop, j = 1 then j = 2.
examples.check:
a = [x*x for x in range(1, 7) if x % 2 == 0]
b = [x if x > 0 else 0 for x in [-2, 3, -1, 5]]
c = [i + j for i in range(1, 3) for j in range(1, 3)]
for v in a + b + c:
    print(v)

traps: The filter comes after the for clause. 'if x % 2 == 0 for x in range(6)' is a SyntaxError; the parser expects the for first.
An if-else must always carry its else. [x if x > 0 for x in data] fails, because that if is read as part of the expression, not as a filter.
Do not confuse the two kinds of if. [x for x in data if x > 0] shortens the list; [x if x > 0 else 0 for x in data] keeps the length and replaces values.
A comprehension returns a new list and never edits the original, even if the expression mentions a name that also points at the old list.
In Python 3 the loop variable belongs to the comprehension's own scope. After [x for x in range(5)], the name x is not defined outside, unlike a plain for loop.

quiz.q: What does [x * 2 for x in range(4)] produce?
quiz.a: range(4) gives 0, 1, 2, 3. Each is doubled, so the list is [0, 2, 4, 6].

quiz.q: In what order do the three parts appear inside the brackets of [expr for item in iterable if cond]?
quiz.a: The expression comes first, then the for clause, then the if clause. Execution still starts with the for clause.

quiz.q: Explain the difference between [x for x in nums if x > 0] and [x if x > 0 else 0 for x in nums].
quiz.a: The first has a filter, so it keeps only the positive items and the result is shorter. The second has a conditional expression, so every item is processed and non-positive items become 0, keeping the length the same.

quiz.q: Why does a list comprehension not change the list it reads from?
quiz.a: The comprehension builds a fresh list object and appends new values to it. It only reads the source iterable, so the source keeps its contents and its identity.

quiz.q: Give the output of [i * j for i in range(1, 4) for j in range(1, 3)].
quiz.a: The first for is outer: i = 1, 2, 3. The inner loop gives j = 1, 2 each time. i = 1 gives 1, 2; i = 2 gives 2, 4; i = 3 gives 3, 6. Output [1, 2, 2, 4, 3, 6].

quiz.q: Write one list comprehension that takes the strings ['10', '20', '35'] and returns only the integer values greater than 15.
quiz.a: [int(s) for s in ['10', '20', '35'] if int(s) > 15]. int('10') = 10 fails the test, int('20') = 20 and int('35') = 35 pass, so the result is [20, 35].

quiz.q: A student writes [x if x % 2 == 0 for x in range(6)] and gets a SyntaxError. Identify the cause and give a corrected line with its output.
quiz.a: The if is written before the for clause, so Python treats it as the start of a conditional expression, and a conditional expression requires else. The filter belongs after the for: [x for x in range(6) if x % 2 == 0], which gives [0, 2, 4].

beyond: Not for the exam. In real data work the same pattern appears everywhere: cleaning a column of strings, converting units, dropping invalid rows before a sum. NumPy, covered in Unit 6, replaces most list comprehensions with vectorised array expressions that run in compiled code and are far faster on lakhs of values. Pandas follows the same idea for whole columns. Code reviewers often ask you to break a long comprehension into a named loop, because a readable loop beats a clever one-liner in a shared codebase. Search for "list comprehension", "nested comprehension readability" and "NumPy vectorisation" to go further.
